(5) Rent-to-Own. One way sellers have gotten 
around regulations 
attempting to protect consumers in credit sales is to lease, rather than sell 
household goods. As described by one court, "the rent-to-own contract i~ 
styled as a lease renewal from week-to-week or month-to-month. Upon 
renewal for the stipulated number of weeks or months, the 'lessee' obtains 
ownership of the personal property. The 'lessee' had the option to terminate 
the lease at any time in this fashion, and can eliminate a financial burden at 
anytime. In return, the consumer ordinarily pays considerably more for the 
item than the retail price and loses any equity that may have accrued before 
termination 
of the agreement if less than all the specified renewals are 
made." Green v. Continental Rentals, 678 A.2d 759 (N.J. Super. 1994). In 
that case the court found that the "rent" was really interest in disguise and 
therefore 
constituted an unconscionable practice 
under New Jersey's 
Consumer Fraud Act. Federal Reserve Board regulations, 
however, exclude 
rent-to-own contracts from the definition of "credit sales" under the Federal 
Truth in Lending Act. See Ortiz v. Rental Management 
Inc., 65 F.3d 335 (3d 
Cir. 1995). 
(6) Price Justification? In an FTC survey of retailing in the District of 
Columbia, sellers catering primarily to low-income customers were found to 
use comparatively high markups and prices, although their "net profit on 
sales ... was only slightly higher and net profit return on net worth was 
considerably lower when compared to general market retailers." Federal 
Trade Commission, Economic Report on Installment 
Credit and Retail Sales 
Practices of District of Columbia Retailers (1968). Should this be a defense to 
a claim of price unconscionability? 
It has been suggested that a price 
exceeding the "average" by 100% be deemed prima facie unconscionable. 
Richard Speidel, Unconscionability, Assent and Consumer Protection, 31 U. 
Pitt. L. Rev. 359, 372-73 (1970). Would it be b tter to focus attention on the 
mark-up of an item than on its price? Should a seller be compelled to produce 
information regarding costs, profits, and mark-ups? See Patterson v. Walker· 
Thomas Furniture Co., 277 A.2d 111 (D.C. App. 1971) Does such disclosure 
have special difficulties in disputes regarding lawrrs' 
fees? See Note 2, 
below.
